#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""plan-moves.py --root WT --base AT [--stale-at REV]: check that every line taken out of PLAN.md went to PLAN-history.md word for word, and list the PLAN lines that look stale.

A line taken out is a line of PLAN.md at AT, the commit that the worktree WT was made at, that the working
PLAN.md no longer holds, as a whole line: a line moved, cut to a pointer, or changed. Each must stand among
the lines that the working PLAN-history.md gained since AT, as many times as it went. PLAN-history.md only
gains: a line that it lost is a failure too. Blank lines are not counted. Prints the counts, the headings
that PLAN-history.md gained, and each failure; exit 1 on any.

Then, for information only (they never fail), the PLAN lines to look at, one `LOOK` line each with its
reason, read against the working review queue and the history of AT:
  settled   a list line whose own pointer, a sentence "Review-queue item 296.", names items that are each
            settled in the queue's part (a), and that names no item open in (b) or (c); it skips a line that
            already carries a cleanup's mark, "closed at the cleanup of DATE" in any of the queue cleanup's
            forms ("(closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05: learning)", "item 127, closed at the cleanup of
            2026-11-05: settled", "are closed at the cleanup of 2026-11-05 (learning)"): the cleanup marked
            it in place, and moving it out of PLAN is PLAN's consolidation, not a landing's change
  list      a list line that names three or more items, some of them settled; or one that ties its items
            to a list of the queue's head (the queue's "Needed before the switch-over") and does not name
            the same items
  finding   a line `- Climb batch N's review, finding M ...` whose finding a commit in the history of AT
            names (`batch-N-review.md, finding M`, or "climb batch N's finding M"), where that commit
            changes a file outside the record: a half of the line may be built
With --stale-at REV, it reads PLAN.md and the review queue at REV, and the history of REV, prints only the
LOOK lines, and exits 0: evidence.py gives them to the sorter in plan.md.
"""
import argparse
import collections
import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys

ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
ap.add_argument('--root', required=True)
ap.add_argument('--base', required=True)
ap.add_argument('--stale-at')
a = ap.parse_args()
D = 'explorations/coordinator/'


def at(rel, rev=None):
    rev = rev or a.base
    r = subprocess.run(['git', '-C', a.root, 'show', '%s:%s' % (rev, D + rel)], capture_output=True, text=True)
    if r.returncode:
        sys.exit('plan-moves.py: no %s at %s' % (rel, rev))
    return r.stdout.split('\n')

- R1: as planned. Not consequential.
- B1 to B3: ordering only.

content.content:
- **Walk** is the interpreter. The **compiled path** checks a program with the **checker** and then writes JVM bytecode with the **code generator**.
- The **prelude** is the small library that the compiled path uses by default. The **one library** is the library of the interpreter.
- The **selector** is the setting `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one`. With it, the compile command reads the one library. A program compiled so does not run yet.
- A **value object** is an object with value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Nothing can extend an object.
- A **payload class** is a small hand-written Java class that holds the bare JVM number, such as an `int`. The code generator writes each number object's class on top of it.
- A **row** is one known defect in the ledger. An **expected-failure test** is a test that is known to fail and is marked so.
- The **gate** is the full check before a run lands.
- A **task** is one change of the run. The record names it a rung. A **worker** is an agent that does one task. A **skeptic** is a second agent that examines the worker's change. A **judge** is a third agent that rules where the skeptic contests a fix.
- A **fork** is a design question with more than one way. A **default** is the way that the record chose before the run.
- A **varargs parameter** takes any number of arguments, written `xs: ZZ32...`.
- A **type assumption**, `e asif T`, makes the call around it choose its declaration as if `e` were a `T`.
- An **arm** is one clause of a `typecase`.
- The **measure** counts the declarations of the one library that the code generator refuses.

**What each task changed.** Each program is shortened from the tests that landed.

- **N. The prelude's seven number types are value objects.** The prelude, the code generator and seven run-time classes changed.

      object MyNum extends ZZ32 end

  - Before: the program compiled. When it ran, the JVM refused the class: 'IncompatibleClassChangeError'.
  - Now: the compile refuses it: 'Invalid type in extends clause: ZZ32'. Walk refuses it too. This is your decision P-178, now on both libraries' text.
  - Also now: `add(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32)` beside `add(a: List, b: List)`, for a program's own trait `List`, compiles and runs. Before, the checker refused it.
  - Also now, one program that compiled is refused:

        kindOf(x: ZZ32): String = typecase x of
            Shape => "shape"
            else => "integer"
          end

    `Shape` is a trait of the program. Before, it printed "integer", as walk does. Now the checker refuses it: 'The typecase clause, Shape, is unreachable.' The team's checker has this rule. The specification has no such rule. It is on your list.
  - Also now: `x: Object = ZZ32` is refused by the code generator. Before, the checker refused it. Walk gives 0. What the name `ZZ32` means as a value is on your list.

- **W. Two hidden functions at one place get two class names.** The code generator changed.

      same(xs: List[\ZZ32\], ys: List[\ZZ32\]): Boolean =
          (|xs| = |ys|) AND: (BIG AND [(a, b) <- xs.zip[\ZZ32\](ys)] a = b)

  - Before: the compile stopped: 'ZipException: duplicate entry'. The compiler makes two hidden functions from that line, at one place in the source, and gave both one name.
  - Now: it compiles, under the prelude and with the selector. The second hidden function's name ends in `#2`. The one library's `=` on lists has this form.

- **G. A function with a varargs parameter compiles with the selector.** The code generator changed.

      count(xs: ZZ32...): ZZ32 = |xs|
      println(count(4, 5, 6))

  - Before, with the selector: the compile stopped: 'Can't compile VarArgs yet'.
  - Now: it compiles. The three arguments become one array that cannot be changed, as under walk. Its run waits until the one library compiles whole.
  - Without the selector it is still refused. The message now names the missing array type.
  - Still wrong on both paths: `count(1, ys...)`, where `ys` holds two numbers, gives 1. It should give 3. The extra arguments are dropped with no message. It is a new row, and no task repairs it yet.

- **R. A method of a trait from another component is found.** The code that gathers a trait's methods changed.

      object O extends B
          tag(self, n: ZZ32): String = "o"
      end

  - `B` is a trait of another component, with `tag(self, s: String)`.
  - Before: the compile stopped: 'Not in the trait table: B'.
  - Now: it compiles and runs. With the selector, a program with an array, `a = array1[\ZZ32, 8\]()`, compiles too.
  - Also now: `stamp(Q asif R, "d")`, where the object `Q` overrides `R`'s `stamp`, runs `R`'s body, as walk and the specification say. Before, it ran `Q`'s.
  - Also now: `("ab" asif String) < ("cd" asif String)` gives false. Before, it gave true. The prelude's `String` has a placeholder `<` that gives false, and the call now runs it. The prelude goes at the switch-over.

All tests passed at the gate, on the first run: 3,608 tests, and no failure. The two measures of the checker on the one library stay at 0. The quick microGPT check passed 7 of 7 for both programs.

**The measure.** Before run 2, the code generator refused 13 declarations of the one library. After run 2, it refuses 1, `__bigOperator2`. The coordinator measured it after the landing.

**The decisions that took the planner's default.** Each one can be undone.

- **Each number type's class is written over its payload class, and every compiled name of the type names the payload class (forks N1 and N3).** The other way named the object's class everywhere and changed every helper. Now each type has one name when a program runs, so two old defects run.
- **The payload class finds its object's class by name, in a small table that follows the selector (fork N2).** The other way was a table that each class fills when it loads, which misses a value made before that.
- **The one library's seven number types take this form later, in the task where the first program runs on the one library (fork N4).** The other way was this task, with no test that can fail. Until then, with the selector, a compiled varargs call would stop when it runs. That task must also cover the varargs indices.
- **A test of the team that pinned one error now pins two (fork N6).** Its program extends `ZZ32` in an object expression, which your decision now refuses.
- **The second hidden function at one place takes its name with `#2`; the first keeps today's name (fork W1).** The other way was a counter for every function, which renames every class.

On the compiled path microGPT's 18 components stop at name resolution until the switch-over (F-97). Under `FORTRESS_LIBRARY=one` the compile command reads the one library, and a program compiled so does not run yet (F-381; row 1062). Nothing of it landed.

-- **The live thread.** Phase 4, the switch-over: one library, the interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks (P-37), the natives first (P-33). At the last landed gate, climb batch 33b's (`ba3c7c876d`, run 2 of climb batch 33, its gate on `f9acd7f6c2`), the distance is 0 and the checker count 0 over the fourteen components, with no crash row (F-53; `compile-ladder/climb-batch-33b/gate/`). Walk loads `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, reading two type parameters whose bounds exclude as never one type, and the checker refuses the pair; `Bottom` lies within both bounds and cannot be written, so which path moves is his. lines: 323. **P-60's coverage against the POPL 2019 paper's Meet Rule: does the meet of two overloads over closed traits stay covered by several declarations, or does it take one declaration, as [Meet-Third] and the paper's theorem of one most specific declaration ask (P-60)?** The rule: a pair whose domains overlap and do not nest needs a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to their meet, [Meet-Third] (`Papers/Variance/rules.tex:57-61`), so that every call has one most specific declaration statically (`thm:mostspecific`, `rules.tex:509-524`). The decision: P-60 lets several declarations below both cover the meet through `comprises` clauses, so a static call may have several most specific declarations, typed by the intersection of their return types, the declaration that runs unique only at run time (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md:57`); the checker builds it for declarations without static parameters (`coverageRule`, `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/OverloadingChecker.scala:676-694`; `coversOverlap`, `scala_src/overloading/OverloadingOracle.scala:188-239`). The type-decisions judgement of 2026-10-23 weighed it: "P-60 is the one step outside the designers' proven model, and it is recorded as such; it stands" (`reviews/type-decisions-review/judgement.md`, V6), and Appendix I says so (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex:3514-3525`). The POPL 2019 rules map, read against the technical report's sources, sets the rule beside P-60 as a decision not taken, with the same two ways (`reviews/popl2019-rules-map.md`, question 2, sections 18 and 23). The Working Draft's passage that the other way cites ends "We agreed to revise the Meet rule to address this with the coverage check." (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:285`), which Appendix I quotes (`changes.tex:3485`).
- Landed: P-60 as it reads, its coverage case built in the checker. Default: P-60 as it reads.

lines: 513. **Which run-time class carries each built-in type of the one library on the compiled path, for the types that P-178 does not cover?** The rehearsal's question, the plan review's, and question 1 of the carriers' review. A carrier is the JVM class whose instances are a built-in type's values, as `FZZ32` for the prelude's `trait ZZ32`. Answered for the five number types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN64` and `RR64` by his decision of 2026-11-16 (P-178; the review's way D): each is one `value object` under its own name, no trait stays above it, and compiled code can hold its value as a bare JVM `int`, `long` or `double` (P-17); `NN32` and `RR32` already have that form. Not open, corrected on 2026-11-16 after the curator asked whether these types had not been discussed before: `value object Boolean` and `value object Char` are objects with no trait in the one library, the form that P-178 gives the numbers, and stay so; the Java-backed traits are decided, `JavaBufferedWriter` and `JavaBufferedReader` by P-164 (his "(b) it is." of 2026-11-06: at the switch-over the run-time classes implement the one library's traits) and the two array stores by P-169 (the Fable judgement that he took on 2026-11-07, with his choice of the slot API on 2026-11-08). For `String` nothing is his to decide, and no new probe is due (corrected again on 2026-11-16, after he said that the record had not been searched; the scout's fourth pass, and the reports themselves). The shape is fixed by his words and decisions: the coordinator's line of 2026-11-05 18:28Z, which he did not contest, "how Fortress strings live on the JVM, the team already decided ... That design stays; nothing on the table reopens it"; his words of 2026-11-07 05:42Z, strings are "user extensible/modifiable reference types", with room "to slip specialized implementation under String trait, like the CatString does"; P-168 and P-171. The work is done in three places: `reviews/carriers-ways-2026-11-13.md`, "On `String`" under each way (`String` is an interface, `FlatString`'s class holds a `java.lang.String`, a wrapper casts a helper's `String` parameter; "This is the same in every way"), and "the two libraries agree"; the rehearsal's wall W2, built in scratch and run (`compile-ladder/plan-31/probes/switch-rehearsal.md`); probe Y's second set of run-time classes (F-353). Left for a builder, with the merge of P-178: the form that gives `FlatString`'s class while it stays an object, the same work as for `Boolean`, `Char`, `NN32`, `RR32` and the merged numbers; F-322's two readings of a helper's `String` parameter; ropes and a program's own `String` compiled, which wait on other rows. For his review at its default: item 466, a string object's ilk keeps `FlatString`. Also the planner's, not his: whether the class of a native object is written by hand over a generated springboard, or by the code generator over a hand-written payload class (the review's way C, forms 1 and 2). The team's sources do not point to one way (F-359, F-379).
